1553A:
**Key insight.** S(x+1) < S(x) exactly when x's last digit is 9 — rolling a trailing 9 (or a run of trailing 9s) over to 0 always shrinks the digit sum, and that's the *only* way a +1 can decrease it.

**Approach.** Count integers in [1, n] ending in digit 9: they are 9, 19, 29, ..., so the count is ⌊(n+1)/10⌋.

**Complexity.** O(1) per query, O(t) total.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Trying to reason digit-by-digit about carries instead of noticing it collapses to "last digit is 9".
- Off-by-one in the counting formula (use ⌊(n+1)/10⌋, not ⌊n/10⌋).
1554A:
**Key insight.** The optimal window [l, r] can always be shrunk to two *adjacent* elements without lowering max·min — so you never need to consider windows wider than 2.

**Approach.** Slide over the array and take the best a[i]·a[i+1] over all adjacent pairs.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Not trusting/proving the adjacent-pair reduction and instead writing an O(n²) scan over all (l, r), which times out on n up to 1e5.
- Forgetting the sum-of-n constraint means the O(n) solution must avoid any per-test-case overhead like re-allocating large structures.
1566A:
**Key insight.** To maximize the median you should zero out the lower ⌊n/2⌋ elements and pour the entire sum s as evenly as possible into the remaining ⌊n/2⌋+1 elements at or above the median position — that group's shared value *is* the median.

**Approach.** Compute k = ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 (the number of "upper" elements) and answer ⌊s / k⌋.

**Complexity.** O(1) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Confusing which half of the array needs the sum — it's the ceil(n/2) elements from the median position upward, not just "half of them".
- Getting the ⌈m/2⌉ median-position definition wrong for even n (it's the *lower* of the two middle elements, not the upper).
1582A:
**Key insight.** Since a ≥ 1 always, there is at least one 1-minute song, which acts as a flexible "adjustment unit" letting you realize any subset-sum parity that the total allows. So the minimum imbalance is determined purely by the total duration's parity.

**Approach.** Total duration T = a + 2b + 3c. Since 2-minute songs never change parity, the achievable minimum difference is T mod 2 — equivalently, 0 if a and c share parity, else 1.

**Complexity.** O(1) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Falling into a combinatorial-explosion of parity cases on (a, b, c) separately (as a naive first attempt tends to), instead of reducing to the single fact that only the *total*'s parity matters.
- Forgetting that 2-minute songs are "free" — they can always be split evenly and never affect the achievable parity.
1591A:
**Key insight.** This is a direct simulation of the four stated growth rules — no cleverness needed, just careful bookkeeping of "missed days in a row".

**Approach.** Walk the days left to right, tracking height and a consecutive-miss counter; on a watered day, add 5 if the previous day was also watered, else add 1, and reset the miss counter; on a missed day, increment the miss counter and stop immediately with -1 once it reaches 2.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Off-by-one when checking "watered on day i AND i−1" — needs an explicit guard for i = 0 (no previous day).
- Continuing to simulate after the flower has died instead of short-circuiting to -1.
1608A:
**Key insight.** Any run of consecutive integers starting at 2 already satisfies the divisibility condition: since a_i − a_{i−1} = 1 and a_{i−1} ≥ 2, a_{i−1} can only divide a_i if a_i = a_{i−1} or a_i ≥ 2·a_{i−1}, and neither holds when they differ by exactly 1.

**Approach.** Output 2, 3, 4, ..., n+1.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Starting the sequence at 1 instead of 2 — 1 divides every integer, instantly breaking the non-divisibility condition for a_2.
- This is a "print any valid answer" constructive problem: many other constructions work (primes, powers of two, ...); don't over-engineer when the simplest one suffices.
1618A:
**Key insight.** After sorting the 7 subsequence sums b, the two smallest entries must be the two smallest original elements (single-element sums are always the smallest sums), and the largest entry is the sum of all three elements.

**Approach.** Sort b; set a1 = b[0], a2 = b[1], and recover a3 as b[6] − a1 − a2 (the reference solution instead scans the remaining five values for one equal to b[6]−a1−a2, which is more defensive but the same idea).

**Complexity.** O(1) per test case (sorting a fixed 7-element list).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Assuming any two of the smallest values are individual elements without relying on the guarantee that a valid array exists — the guarantee is what makes this reconstruction safe.
- Index confusion among the fixed 7 sums; it helps to explicitly label which subsequence each position could correspond to.
1619A:
**Key insight.** A string of length n is square iff n is even and its first half equals its second half — nothing more subtle than that.

**Approach.** Check n % 2 == 0, then compare s[:n/2] to s[n/2:].

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting the immediate odd-length rejection.
- Using an indirect check like counting occurrences of the first half as a substring (works, but a direct slice comparison is clearer and just as fast — prefer it).
1620A:
**Key insight.** Treat 'E' edges as merging neighboring positions into groups around the circle (a union-find). An 'N' edge just requires its two neighboring groups to differ. This is unsatisfiable *only* when there is exactly one 'N': with all other edges 'E', the single long E-chain wraps the whole circle into one group on both sides of that lone N, forcing the group to differ from itself.

**Approach.** Count the 'N' characters: answer is NO iff the count is exactly 1, YES otherwise (0 N's → everything can be one value; ≥2 N's → the circle splits into ≥2 independent groups, each assignable a distinct value, satisfying every N automatically).

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Reaching for an N-count *parity* / bipartite-coloring argument — that pattern applies to "must differ from neighbor" graphs in general, but here 'E' constraints collapse whole runs into single groups first, which is what breaks the usual parity intuition.
- Off-by-one when treating the array as circular (the last constraint wraps a_n to a_1).
1622A:
**Key insight.** After breaking one stick you need two matching pairs among the four pieces. That happens in exactly two shapes: either one stick's length already equals the sum of the other two (break it into those two exact pieces), or two sticks are already equal and the third is even (split it into equal halves).

**Approach.** Check the three "one stick = sum of the other two" cases, then the three "two sticks equal and the third is even" cases.

**Complexity.** O(1) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting the evenness check when two sticks are already equal — an odd third stick can't be split into two equal integer pieces.
- Missing the "stick equals sum of other two" case entirely and only checking the equal-pair case.
1559B:
**Key insight.** A blank cell should simply be colored to differ from an already-decided neighbor — this greedy choice never costs you anything later, since it locally removes a same-color pair without constraining future cells any more than leaving it blank would.

**Approach.** Sweep left to right, carrying forward the color of the last resolved cell; whenever you hit a '?', set it to the opposite of that carried color (default to alternating B/R if the whole string is blank). One linear pass suffices.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Repeatedly rescanning and "radiating" from every fixed cell until no '?' remains (as a first-draft solution might) — correct at these sizes but needlessly O(n²); a single left-to-right carry is the clean O(n) version.
- Forgetting the all-blank case still needs an explicit alternating pattern.
1582B:
**Key insight.** The elements you *drop* to form the subsequence must sum to exactly 1. Since every a_i is a non-negative integer, that forces the dropped set to be exactly one element equal to 1, plus any subset of the elements equal to 0 — no element ≥ 2 can ever be part of it.

**Approach.** Let n1 = count of elements equal to 1 and n0 = count of elements equal to 0. Each of the n1 ones can be "the" dropped one, and independently each of the n0 zeros may or may not also be dropped, giving n1 · 2^n0 distinct nearly-full subsequences.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting that dropping different subsets of the zero-elements still counts as different subsequences even though the sum condition doesn't care about them.
- Assuming two larger elements could combine to a dropped-sum of 1 — impossible with non-negative integers other than a lone 1.
1567B:
**Key insight.** Any array with MEX = a must contain each of 0..a−1 at least once, and that mandatory core has a fixed XOR, f(a). If f(a) already equals the target b, a elements suffice. Otherwise you need one more element x = f(a) ⊕ b to fix the XOR — except when x happens to equal a itself, since adding the value a would push the MEX up to a+1; that case needs two extra elements instead.

**Approach.** Compute f(a) = XOR(0..a−1) with the standard O(1) closed form (period-4 pattern), compare it to b, and answer a, a+1, or a+2 depending on whether f(a) equals b, f(a)⊕b equals a, or neither.

**Complexity.** O(1) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Missing the x == a collision case — it's the entire crux of the problem, not an edge case to bolt on after the fact.
- Off-by-one between XOR(0..a−1) and XOR(0..a) when deriving the closed form.
1569B:
**Key insight.** Type-1 (no-loss) players can simply draw every game. Type-2 (needs ≥1 win) players must win at least one game, and the only games where a decisive result is possible without hurting anyone are games *between two type-2 players*. So this is only solvable when there are 0 type-2 players, or ≥3 of them (enough to arrange a cycle where each beats at least one other); exactly 1 or 2 type-2 players is always impossible.

**Approach.** Count the type-2 players. If the count is 1 or 2, print NO. Otherwise, draw every game involving a type-1 player, and among the type-2 players arrange results (e.g. each beats the next one in a cyclic order) so every one of them secures at least one win.

**Complexity.** O(n²) to build and print the result matrix.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Not checking the count-of-1-or-2 impossibility case at all, and instead trying to force a win for a lone type-2 player against a type-1 player (type-1 players can never afford a loss).
- Off-by-one when wiring up the "beat the next player" cycle among type-2 players.
1598B:
**Key insight.** Only 5 candidate days exist, so brute-force every pair of days directly. A pair (a, b) works iff every student is available on at least one of the two days (their union covers everyone) *and* each day individually has enough available students to fill half the class.

**Approach.** For each of the C(5,2)=10 day pairs, check that |available(a) ∪ available(b)| == n and both |available(a)| ≥ n/2 and |available(b)| ≥ n/2 (students available on both days can be assigned to whichever group still needs filling).

**Complexity.** O(10·n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Checking only the ≥ n/2 count condition without also checking full coverage (or vice versa) — both are necessary, neither alone is sufficient.
- Forgetting a student could be available on neither of the two chosen days, which immediately disqualifies that pair.
1622B:
**Key insight.** Once you decide liked songs take the top ranks and disliked songs take the bottom ranks, minimizing total |p_i − q_i| never benefits from reordering two songs *within* the same group relative to each other — preserving each group's original relative order (by p) and assigning consecutive ranks is always at least as good.

**Approach.** Sort all indices by (liked/disliked, p_i): disliked songs get ranks 1..(count of disliked) in increasing order of their p_i, liked songs get the remaining top ranks, also in increasing order of their p_i.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Assigning disliked songs the high ranks and liked songs the low ranks (backwards from the requirement).
- Reordering within a group arbitrarily instead of preserving relative p-order, which needlessly inflates the total displacement.
1575A:
**Key insight.** "asc-desc" order is just ordinary ascending lexicographic order after mirroring every character at an even (1-indexed) position through the alphabet (c → 'A' + 'Z' − c) — the mirror exactly flips the comparison direction on those positions, turning "descending on even positions" back into "ascending".

**Approach.** Transform each string by mirroring its even-position characters, sort the transformed strings lexicographically while keeping track of original indices, then output the indices in sorted order.

**Complexity.** O(n·m·log n), dominated by comparing transformed strings during the sort.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Mixing up 1-indexed "odd/even position" from the statement with 0-indexed string access in code.
- Forgetting the mirror transform is only a comparison trick — the final output is still the original indices, not the transformed strings.
1594B:
**Key insight.** A special number is a sum of *distinct* powers of n, which puts special numbers in direct bijection with binary numbers: writing the base-n digits of a special number as 0/1 is exactly the binary representation of its rank in the increasing order.

**Approach.** Write k in binary; treat that bit pattern as the base-n digit pattern of the answer, i.e. answer = Σ n^i over every set bit i of k, evaluated with fast modular exponentiation.

**Complexity.** O(log k) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Applying the modulus too early and letting it corrupt which powers of n get selected — only the final summed value needs to be taken mod 1e9+7, the bit-selection logic itself is exact.
- Confusing "k in binary" (which selects which powers of n are used) with iterating k times.
1604B:
**Key insight.** Splitting every element into its own singleton subarray gives h_i = 1 for all i, so the XOR of all of them is 0 exactly when n is even — meaning n even is *always* a YES via this trivial split. For odd n, that trivial split leaves XOR = 1, but merging any single non-increasing adjacent pair (a[i] ≥ a[i+1]) into one block keeps that block's LIS at 1 (a non-increasing pair has no increasing subsequence of length 2) while dropping the block count to the even n−1 — flipping the XOR back to 0. The only truly impossible case is odd n with a strictly increasing array, where every contiguous block's LIS equals its own length and no such fix exists.

**Approach.** If n is even, print YES. Otherwise scan for any i with a[i] ≥ a[i+1]; print YES if found, NO otherwise.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Assuming merging any adjacent pair keeps its LIS at 1 — that's only true for a *non-increasing* pair; merging an increasing pair gives LIS 2 and breaks the parity trick.
- Missing the trivial "all singletons" split for even n and instead searching for something more complicated.
1618C:
**Key insight.** A valid d must alternate red/blue strictly by position, so it has to divide every element at one parity of positions (all evens or all odds) and divide none at the other parity — which means the only candidates worth testing are the GCD of the even-position elements and the GCD of the odd-position elements (any smaller divisor is strictly more likely to also divide something in the opposite class, never less).

**Approach.** Compute g_even = gcd of elements at even positions and g_odd = gcd of elements at odd positions. Try d = g_even (valid if g_even > 1 and no odd-position element is divisible by it); if that fails, try d = g_odd symmetrically; otherwise print 0.

**Complexity.** O(n log(max a_i)) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Checking only that the candidate divides its own class, forgetting to also verify it divides *none* of the opposite class.
- Trying arbitrary divisors instead of the GCD — the GCD is provably the best (most permissive) candidate for its class.
1623B:
**Key insight.** Process Alice's recorded ranges from smallest (most nested) to largest. A range's split point d is the one integer in [l, r] not covered by any already-resolved smaller range nested inside it — concretely, d sits immediately after the rightmost "left child" range and immediately before the leftmost "right child" range recorded within [l, r].

**Approach.** Sort ranges by length ascending. For each range [l, r], find the largest right-endpoint among already-placed ranges sharing its left endpoint l (call its end L) and the smallest left-endpoint among already-placed ranges sharing its right endpoint r (call its start R); d = L+1 if only a left child exists, d = R−1 if only a right child exists, d = l = r if neither exists, and d = (L+1+R-1)/2's single integer gap between them if both exist (that gap is always exactly one cell wide).

**Complexity.** O(n²) per test case with direct pairwise matching (n ≤ 1000 total, so this is fast enough); an O(n log n) stack-based version also exists.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Processing ranges in input order instead of by nesting size — the whole approach depends on resolving children before parents.
- Off-by-one when computing the single gap cell between a left child and a right child.
1559C:
**Key insight.** Villages 1..n already form a path via the i→i+1 roads; village n+1 just needs to be spliced in at the one place where an *incoming* road (some k with a_k=0, i.e. k→n+1) is immediately followed by an *outgoing* road (a_{k+1}=1, i.e. n+1→k+1). If the very last village n has a_n=0, no splicing is even needed — just append n+1 at the end.

**Approach.** If a[n]=0, output 1, 2, ..., n, n+1. Otherwise scan backward for the largest k with a_k=0 (guaranteed to exist, with a_{k+1}=1 since a_n=1), and output 1, ..., k, n+1, k+1, ..., n.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Splicing at a point where the incoming/outgoing edge directions don't actually match (need a_k=0 for k→n+1 and a_{k+1}=1 for n+1→k+1, not the reverse).
- Missing the simpler "just append at the end" case and always doing a full backward scan.
1582C:
**Key insight.** Since you may only erase copies of one chosen letter, fix a candidate letter and scan from both ends inward: positions that already match can be skipped for free; whenever the two ends mismatch, one of them *must* be the chosen letter (erase it and advance just that pointer) — if neither mismatched character is the chosen letter, that choice is impossible.

**Approach.** For each of the (at most 26) letters present in s, run a two-pointer scan from both ends counting forced erasures on mismatch; take the minimum count over all letters that succeed, or -1 if none do.

**Complexity.** O(26·n) total (each letter costs one O(n) two-pointer pass).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting that when *both* mismatched characters equal the chosen letter, either one may be erased (they're symmetric, either choice works).
- Not handling the single-distinct-character string as an automatic 0 before running the general scan.
1586B:
**Key insight.** In a star graph (every node connected directly to one fixed center), no node ever lies strictly between two others — every simple path has at most one interior node, the center itself. So restrictions are trivially satisfied as long as the center you pick was never named as a forbidden "middle" node b in any restriction.

**Approach.** Mark every node that appears as the b in some restriction; since there are only m < n restrictions, at least one node is never marked — pick any unmarked node as the center and connect every other node to it directly.

**Complexity.** O(n + m) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Picking an arbitrary center without checking it wasn't named as a forbidden middle node.
- Overcomplicating the construction (trying to satisfy restrictions individually) instead of noticing the star shape sidesteps all of them structurally.
1608B:
**Key insight.** Local maxima and minima must alternate along any permutation, so a and b can differ by at most 1, and together they need a+b ≤ n−2 interior slots to fit in. When feasible, alternately placing the smallest and largest remaining values produces a peak or valley at every interior step of that zigzag; once you've produced exactly a peaks and b valleys, finish with the remaining values in one monotonic run (which contributes no further extrema).

**Approach.** Reject if |a−b| > 1 or a+b > n−2. Otherwise build a zigzag of length a+b+2 alternating smallest/largest remaining values (starting with whichever side yields the correct first extremum type), append the rest of the values as a plain increasing or decreasing run, and verify the peak/valley counts before printing.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Getting the "start with a peak or a valley" choice backwards, which shifts every subsequent extremum's type.
- Off-by-one on the interior-slot bound — only positions 2..n−1 can be local extrema, giving n−2 usable slots, not n−1 or n.
1613C:
**Key insight.** Total damage dealt is monotonically non-decreasing in k (a longer poison duration never deals less damage), so binary search on k works directly.

**Approach.** Binary search k over [1, h]. For a fixed k, total damage = Σ min(gap_i, k) over consecutive attack gaps, plus k for the final attack's unbounded tail (its poison isn't cut short by a following attack); find the smallest k whose total reaches h.

**Complexity.** O(n log h) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting the last attack's contribution is capped only by k itself, not by a following gap.
- Skipping the monotonicity argument and trying to derive k directly from sorted gaps without checking the binary-search predicate is correct (it's easy to get the tie-breaking wrong when the reachable-h point falls exactly between two attacks).
1556B:
**Key insight.** A valid final array alternates parity, which forces one of exactly two "shapes" (evens at even indices / odds at odd indices, or the reverse); for odd n, whichever parity has the majority count is forced into the majority-count slots. Once the target shape is fixed, the minimum adjacent-swap count is the total displacement of just one parity class into its target slots — the opposite-parity elements passively shift to fill the gaps at no extra cost.

**Approach.** Count evens/odds and reject impossible splits. For the (at most two) feasible target shapes, walk the array left to right; for the k-th occurrence of the tracked parity at original index i, its target index is 2k (or 2k+1), so accumulate Σ|target − i|; take the cheaper of the two shapes when both are legal.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Trying to simulate actual swaps instead of realizing the answer is a closed-form sum of displacements for one parity class.
- Missing the -1 impossibility check (parity counts that can't be split into the required slot counts).
1560D:
**Key insight.** Every reachable target is some power of two whose digit string can be produced by deleting digits from n anywhere and appending digits only at the very end — so for a candidate power of two T, the cheapest way to reach it is to greedily match T's digits as a subsequence of n's digits (left to right), delete everything in n that wasn't part of that match, and append whatever's left of T after the match runs out.

**Approach.** For every power of two up to roughly 2^60 (n has ≤10 digits but you may need to append many), greedily subsequence-match its digit string against n's digits; cost = (unmatched digits of n, i.e. deletions) + (unmatched digits of T, i.e. appends). Take the minimum over all candidates.

**Complexity.** O(60 · len(n)) — cheap, since there are ~60 relevant powers of two and n has at most 10 digits.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Not searching far enough into large powers of two — since appends are unlimited but only happen at the end, some inputs are cheapest reached via a much larger power of two.
- Overlooking that greedy left-to-right subsequence matching is optimal here (matching as early as possible only ever helps, never hurts, later matches).
1591C:
**Key insight.** A round trip that mixes depots on both sides of the origin is never better than handling each side separately (you pass through the origin either way), and since you can carry k bags per trip, it's always best to let each necessary trip also carry along whichever *closer* bags on that side are still waiting — so trips should be grouped from the farthest depot inward in batches of k. The one exception: the very last delivery of the entire day never needs a return trip, so you get to subtract one one-way leg at the end.

**Approach.** Split into positive-side and negative-side depots, sort each side by distance from the origin. Walking from the farthest point inward in steps of k, add 2×(batch's farthest distance) per batch on each side (round trip). Finally subtract the smaller of the two sides' farthest-batch distances once, since the globally last delivery only costs a one-way trip.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) per test case (sorting).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting the final one-way-trip discount entirely, or applying it to the wrong (farther) side.
- Mixing positive and negative depots into the same batches instead of treating the two sides independently.
1594E1:
**Key insight.** Fix the root's color (6 choices). Every other node's valid colors depend only on its own parent's color, and — because the Rubik's-cube adjacency graph is symmetric — *every* color has exactly 4 valid neighbor colors (6 total, minus itself, minus its one forbidden opposite face). So each non-root node independently contributes a factor of 4, regardless of which color its parent actually took.

**Approach.** Answer = 6 · 4^(number of non-root nodes) mod 1e9+7. A perfect binary tree of k levels has 2^k − 1 nodes, so the exponent is 2^k − 2; compute it with fast modular exponentiation (or, equivalently, multiply in 4^(nodes at each level) level by level, as the reference solution does).

**Complexity.** O(log k) with fast exponentiation (or O(k) building the product level by level).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Assuming the "4 valid neighbors" count varies by color and trying to case-split on it — the structure is fully symmetric, it doesn't.
- Off-by-one on the node count (2^k − 1 total, so 2^k − 2 *non-root* nodes).
1604C:
**Key insight.** An element's index can only ever decrease over time (as earlier elements get erased, everything shifts left), never increase — so once you fix the order elements get removed in, each surviving element eventually faces a *shrinking* set of possible positions, and therefore a *growing* set of "must not be divisible by (position+1)" constraints. In particular, the first element can never move, so if a_1 is even the answer is immediately NO.

**Approach.** Maintain a running value x = lcm of all positions+1 seen so far (starting at 2). Walk the array in order: if the current element is divisible by x, output NO immediately (it can never dodge that constraint); otherwise fold the next position into x = lcm(x, position+2), and stop updating once x exceeds 1e9 (no element can ever be divisible by something that large again, so the rest are automatically safe). If nothing fails, output YES.

**Complexity.** O(n log(max a_i)) per test case, effectively capped by the early exit once x > 1e9.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Missing the early-exit once the running LCM exceeds 1e9 — without it the LCM can grow needlessly (though it still terminates, it obscures why the algorithm is safe).
- Not seeing why indices only shrink, which is the entire reason later elements accumulate stricter constraints instead of independent ones.
1618D:
**Key insight.** The n−2k *smallest* elements should never be touched — pulling a small element into an operation can only ever save you from adding it verbatim (best case a saving of that small value), while operations are far more valuable spent controlling which *large* elements collide with each other. So sort ascending, leave the bottom n−2k elements alone, and focus all k operations on the top 2k elements. Within that top window, floor-division against a strictly larger partner is free (0), so the only unavoidable cost comes from a value so frequent within the window that, by pigeonhole, some copies of it are forced to pair with each other (⌊x/x⌋ = 1).

**Approach.** Sort the array; sum the smallest n−2k elements directly. Split the remaining top-2k window in half (k smallest-of-the-top vs k largest-of-the-top) and pair index i of the lower half with index i of the upper half — this spreads out any repeated value as evenly as possible across the pairing, which is optimal. Equivalently, if max1 is the most frequent value's count within the top-2k window, the unavoidable extra cost is max(0, 2·max1 − 2k) / 2 forced equal-pairs, each contributing 1.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) per test case (sorting).

**Common pitfalls.**
- The tempting-but-wrong greedy of pairing the k *globally* smallest values against the k *globally* largest values (spanning the untouched elements too) — it matches on some small examples but is provably suboptimal in general (e.g. n=4,k=2,a=[1,3,3,7]: that pairing gives cost 1, but the correct top-window pairing gives 0).
- Forgetting that a repeated large value can force unavoidable ⌊x/x⌋=1 contributions — not every pair in the top window floors to 0 for free.
1549C:
**Key insight.** A noble x is doomed to die *eventually* if and only if x has at least one friend with strictly higher power — regardless of how many lower-power friends currently "protect" it. This holds by induction on power, ascending: every lower-power friend of x is itself connected to x (a higher-power friend), so by induction that friend is doomed too and will eventually vanish, stripping x's protection and exposing it to its higher-power friend. Conversely, if all of x's friends have lower power, that stays true for any surviving subset of them, so x is safe forever.

**Approach.** Maintain a[x] = number of currently-active friendships where x is the lower-power endpoint (i.e. that friend has higher power), updated in O(1) on every add/remove query. The answer to a type-3 query is n minus the count of nobles with a[x] > 0 — no simulation needed.

**Complexity.** O(1) per query, O(n + m + q) total.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Trying to simulate the elimination rounds directly (conceptually straightforward but far too slow across up to 2·10^5 queries).
- Missing that the criterion is purely "has any higher-power friend, ever" — not something that needs to account for which specific friends are still alive.
1600J:
**Key insight.** Each tile's 4-bit code is literally its (North, East, South, West) wall flags — two adjacent cells belong to the same room exactly when there's no wall on the side connecting them, so this is a plain flood-fill / connected-components problem on the grid.

**Approach.** Decode each cell's bitmask into 4 booleans, then run DFS/BFS from every unvisited cell, only stepping into a neighbor when the current cell's bit toward that direction says "no wall"; record each component's size. Sort the sizes descending and print them.

**Complexity.** O(n·m) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Mixing up the N/E/S/W bit order when decoding, or the matching row/column deltas — an easy off-by-one that silently produces a wrong (but plausible-looking) grid graph.
- Forgetting the walls are guaranteed consistent, so only the current cell's own bit needs checking, not both cells sharing an edge.
1562C:
**Key insight.** k = 0 or k = 1 are the easiest targets to engineer: f(t) = f(w)·0 just needs f(t) = 0 (an all-zero substring), and f(t) = f(w)·1 just needs two substrings with the *same* value — which two structural facts about binary values make trivial to construct: a leading zero contributes nothing, so a substring starting exactly at a '0' has the same value as itself with that leading zero dropped (two different-length, equal-value substrings for free); and appending one more '0' bit to any prefix exactly doubles its value (a free k = 2 relationship).

**Approach.** If s has a '0' at 1-indexed position x with x > ⌊n/2⌋, use the prefix-doubling trick: t = [1, x], w = [1, x−1] gives f(t) = 2·f(w). Otherwise, use the leading-zero-drop trick centered on that zero (or, if s is all ones, exploit that every length-⌊n/2⌋ window of an all-ones string has the identical value, so any two such windows trivially satisfy f(t) = f(w)).

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting the ⌊n/2⌋ minimum-length constraint when deciding which of the two zero-based constructions is still legal.
- Overlooking that k is allowed to be 0, which is what makes an all-zero substring an instant, trivial win whenever one exists.
1569C:
**Key insight.** The whole discussion lasts exactly m = max(a) rounds, and a permutation fails to be "nice" precisely when one person ends up as the *sole* remaining speaker for two or more consecutive rounds at the very end — which can only happen if that person uniquely holds the maximum task count and leads the next-highest holder by at least 2 rounds. If two or more people tie for the maximum, no one is ever left alone long enough to violate the rule, so every permutation is automatically nice.

**Approach.** Let m = max(a). If more than one person has a_i = m, the answer is n! (all permutations work). If nobody has a_i = m−1 (the unique leader's nearest rival trails by ≥2), the answer is 0. Otherwise, with c = count of people at a_i = m−1, use inclusion-exclusion over the max-holder's position relative to those c near-max holders (via precomputed factorials/inverse factorials mod 998244353) to count permutations that keep the leader's tail-end solo streak to at most one round.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case with precomputed factorials for O(1) combinations.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Missing either shortcut (tied maximum ⇒ always nice; no one at m−1 ⇒ always impossible) and trying to run the general inclusion-exclusion on them anyway.
- This is a genuinely intricate combinatorial argument — work small examples by hand (n=2,3) before trusting a derived formula.
1575J:
**Key insight.** Simulating each ball step by step is too slow when a long chain of already-triggered "fall straight down" cells exists (each cell's direction changes to 2 the first time any ball passes through it, and after that it's a fixed vertical corridor). Since that transition happens at most once per cell, a Disjoint Set Union that links each visited cell to the one below it lets later balls skip an entire already-traversed vertical run in near O(1) amortized time.

**Approach.** For each ball, repeatedly: DSU-find to jump straight down through any already-visited vertical chain to the first still-"fresh" cell; if that cell's direction is 1 or 3, move left/right accordingly and mark the cell as visited (union it to the cell below); repeat until the ball falls off the grid, then record the final column.

**Complexity.** O((n·m + k)·α(n·m)) total, near-linear thanks to DSU path compression.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Skipping straight to the DSU jump without still applying the real horizontal move at the one "fresh" branching cell each step actually lands on.
- Off-by-one converting between (row, col) and the flattened 1-D DSU index.
1566D2:
**Key insight.** Within a tie-group (people sharing the same sight level), seats can be assigned in any order relative to each other, and the *only* unavoidable inconvenience comes from someone with a smaller arrival index (an earlier person) ending up in a seat *after* (to the right of) a later-arriving groupmate's seat in the same row — i.e., inversions between arrival order and assigned-seat order, restricted to people sharing a row.

**Approach.** Process people in non-decreasing sight order, assigning seats row by row; within a tie-group, use a Fenwick tree (BIT) per row to count, for each newly-seated person, how many already-seated occupants of that row have a smaller seat number but a larger arrival index (an inversion) — sum these counts as people are inserted in arrival order.

**Complexity.** O(n·m·log(n·m)) using per-row Fenwick trees — this is what separates the "hard version" (n up to 300, needing an efficient tie-breaking scheme) from an O((nm)²) brute force.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Computing inversions against seat *number* order instead of *arrival* order (person index 1..nm) — it's the mismatch between the two orderings that creates inconvenience, not either order alone.
- Forgetting inconvenience only accumulates within a single row — cross-row seat assignments never interact.
1623C:
**Key insight.** Whether a target minimum m is achievable is monotonic — if m works, any smaller m′ also works (just leave surplus stones unmoved) — so binary search on the answer. For a *fixed* m, checking feasibility is a unique greedy: process heaps from the last one down to the 3rd, and at each heap donate the maximum possible amount onward while keeping it at ≥ m, since a heap can only ever send stones to its left and never receives anything back once processed, so being maximally generous now never hurts later heaps.

**Approach.** Binary search m over [min(h), max(h)]. Feasibility check: for i from n down to 3, let d = ⌊(h_i − m)/3⌋ (0 if h_i < m, which fails immediately); move d to heap i−1 and 2d to heap i−2; after processing, verify heap 1 and heap 2 are both ≥ m.

**Complexity.** O(n log(max h)) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Donating less than the greedy maximum at some heap, thinking a more "balanced" split could help — it can't, since leftover stones on heap i are wasted the instant heap i is done being processed.
- Forgetting stones only ever flow right-to-left, so a heap already processed can never be topped back up.
1551D1:
**Key insight.** With rows n and columns m, whichever dimension is *odd* forces a structural minimum: an odd number of lines in one direction always needs at least one full line's worth of dominoes running the *other* direction to absorb the leftover, and everything else reduces to a parity constraint on how many dominoes go which way.

**Approach.** Let total = n·m/2. If both n and m are even: feasible iff k (horizontal count) is even — no threshold needed. If n is odd: feasible iff (total − k) is even AND k ≥ ⌊m/2⌋ (at least one full horizontal row's worth is mandatory). If m is odd: feasible iff k is even AND (total − k) ≥ ⌊n/2⌋ (the symmetric case, at least one full vertical column's worth of vertical dominoes).

**Complexity.** O(1) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Swapping which dimension's parity governs which threshold — n odd ties its threshold to ⌊m/2⌋, not ⌊n/2⌋ (it's remarkably easy to mix these up; even careless reference solutions rename the input variables and trip over this).
- Applying a threshold in the "both even" case when none is needed there — that case is pure parity, no minimum count required.
1618E:
**Key insight.** Writing out how each town's total (b_i) relates to its neighbor's (b_{i+1}) collapses the messy staircase of concert durations into one clean linear relationship: b_{i+1} − b_i = S − n·a_{i+1}, where S = Σa_i — because every singer's contribution to town i+1 is either their contribution to town i plus a_i (if they haven't reached home yet) or reset down to a_i (the one singer whose home is i+1). Summing that relationship over all n singers isolates a_{i+1} directly once S is known.

**Approach.** S = (Σ b_i) / (n(n+1)/2) — check this divides evenly first. Then recover each a_i = (S + b_i − b_{i+1}) / n (indices mod n, i.e. town n compares against town 1). Verify every recovered a_i is a positive integer; if any check fails at any stage, print NO.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Getting the index shift backwards (a_i comes from comparing b_i to its *next* town, with the last one wrapping around to the first) — an off-by-one here silently produces a plausible-looking but wrong array.
- Checking only the initial divisibility of the total sum and skipping the per-element integrality/positivity check on every recovered a_i.
1552C:
**Key insight.** Two chords intersect exactly when their endpoints interleave around the circle. The k fixed chords are locked in, but pairing up the remaining free points is entirely up to us — and pairing them by splitting the free-points list (in circular order) exactly in half and matching position i with position i + half maximizes how often the new chords cross both each other and the fixed ones.

**Approach.** Mark the endpoints used by the k fixed chords; collect the unused points in circular order into a list of length 2(n−k); pair index i with index i + (n−k) to form the remaining chords. Then, since n ≤ 100, just directly count all pairwise chord intersections via an interleaving-endpoints check.

**Complexity.** O(n²) per test case (both construction and the final brute-force intersection count).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Pairing free points with their nearest neighbor instead of their "opposite half" partner — that minimizes new crossings instead of maximizing them, exactly backwards.
- Forgetting the final count needs to include crossings between new chords and the original fixed ones, not just crossings among the new chords.
1556C:
**Key insight.** Track a stack of currently-open, unmatched '(' runs; when a ')' run arrives it consumes open runs from the top of the stack (most-recently-opened first, since brackets nest). Whenever a chunk of a '(' run gets closed off, it doesn't just create trivially-nested regular subsegments — it also *glues onto* whatever complete regular-subsegment count already sat immediately before that '(' run opened, creating a batch of new longer valid subsegments that span both pieces.

**Approach.** Maintain a stack of (position, remaining count) for open '(' runs and a running "regular subsegments ending here" tally per position. For each ')' run, pop/partially consume from the stack; each time a '(' run segment closes, add both its own nested contribution and the product/sum with the previously-accumulated regular count immediately to its left. Sum all contributions.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case — each compressed run is pushed and popped from the stack a bounded number of times overall, despite individual run lengths being up to 1e9.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Counting only the obviously-nested matches and missing the extra regular subsegments formed by concatenating a newly-closed block onto an adjacent already-complete regular run — that's where most of the answer comes from.
- Attempting to simulate the actual (possibly gigantic) expanded bracket string instead of working directly with the compressed run-lengths.
1591D:
**Key insight.** A 3-cycle is an even permutation (it decomposes into two transpositions), so any sequence of 3-cycles can only ever reach permutations of *even* parity relative to the identity — unless the array has a repeated value, in which case swapping two equal elements is a free no-op transposition that lets you flip parity at will, making every permutation (odd or even) reachable.

**Approach.** If the array has any duplicate value, print YES immediately. Otherwise it's a genuine permutation of 1..n: compute its parity via cycle decomposition (parity = (n − number of cycles) mod 2) and print YES iff that parity is even.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Forgetting the duplicate-value shortcut and reporting NO on arrays that are actually always sortable because a repeated element supplies a free parity flip.
- Computing parity via inversion counting (correct but needlessly O(n log n)) instead of the simpler O(n) cycle-count formula.
1620E:
**Key insight.** Processing "replace all x with y" queries forward against an already-built array is expensive (each one can touch many elements). Reading the queries *backward* sidesteps this entirely: each array element's final value only depends on the chain of replacements that happen *after* it was inserted, so resolving that chain in reverse — before you ever need to output anything — turns every query into O(1) work.

**Approach.** Initialize ident[v] = v for every possible value. Scan queries from last to first: on a reversed "2 x y", set ident[x] = ident[y] (anything that used to map to x now follows wherever y currently resolves); on a reversed "1 x", record ident[x] as that position's final array value. Reverse the collected values at the end to restore chronological order.

**Complexity.** O(q) total (plus initializing the ident array up to the value bound).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Applying the naive forward approach — looping over the whole array to replace every x with y on each type-2 query — which is O(q²) worst case and far too slow.
- Setting ident[x] = y directly instead of ident[x] = ident[y] — that misses chained replacements that were themselves already redirected earlier in the reverse scan.
1558C:
**Key insight.** Reversing an odd-length prefix never changes any element's position parity: inside a reversed prefix of odd length p, position i maps to p+1−i, which always shares i's parity because p is odd. So a necessary condition for sortability is that every value already sits at a position of matching parity (a_i and i share parity, 1-indexed) — and when that holds, a constructive "selection sort from the top" using a bounded handful of reversals per pair of values fits comfortably inside the 5n/2 budget.

**Approach.** First check a_i % 2 == i % 2 for every i; if any position fails, output -1. Otherwise repeatedly take the current largest unplaced pair of values (k, k−1) and use a short fixed sequence of prefix reversals (bring k to the front, bring k−1 next to it in the correct relative order, then fold the working prefix to drop both into their final two slots) — each round disposes of two values using O(1) reversals.

**Complexity.** O(n) reversals total; O(n²) time with naive position lookups, which is fine for n ≤ 2021.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Skipping the parity precheck and diving straight into the construction — it's the single necessary-and-sufficient condition for feasibility once satisfied, and catching it first avoids wasted work on unsolvable cases.
- Forgetting only *odd*-length prefixes are legal reversal targets when designing each fix-up step.
1599C:
**Key insight.** The probability of playing a studied map, as a function of s (maps studied), is a fixed combinatorial formula that is monotonically non-decreasing in s — so despite the "ternary search" tag, this is really a job for plain binary search (ternary search is for unimodal functions with a single peak; a monotonic function calls for binary search instead).

**Approach.** Derive P(s) by casework on how many of the 3 randomly shown maps are studied: 3 or 2 studied both guarantee a studied map gets played; exactly 1 studied succeeds with probability exactly 1/2 (only half of the equally-likely ways the two players discard the other two maps leave the studied one standing); 0 studied never succeeds. Combine via C(s,3), C(s,2)(n−s), and ½·s·C(n−s,2), all divided by C(n,3). Binary search the smallest s with P(s) ≥ target.

**Complexity.** O(log n) per test case.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Reaching for ternary search out of habit because of the problem's tag instead of recognizing the monotonicity that makes binary search the right (and simpler) tool.
- Getting the "exactly 1 studied map" case's 1/2 probability wrong — it's the single trickiest piece of the derivation, easy to either drop or double-count.
1619F:
**Key insight.** Fairness only requires a single, never-reset rotating pointer through the player list, continuing across every one of the k games rather than restarting each game — because a player's "extra" big-table credit comes purely from where the pointer happens to be when it crosses a large/small table boundary, and an unbroken rotation spreads that offset evenly across everyone over many games.

**Approach.** Compute how many tables must be "large" (⌈n/m⌉ seats) vs "small" (⌊n/m⌋ seats) to seat exactly n people each game. Maintain one pointer into the 1..n player list that is never reset between games; each game, consume the next contiguous block of players into the large tables first, then continue consuming into the small tables, wrapping the pointer mod n as needed.

**Complexity.** O(nk) total (or O(n+k) amortized per test case, one pass through all seatings).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Resetting the rotating pointer to 0 at the start of every game — this silently breaks the fairness guarantee, since the whole scheme relies on the pointer's continuity across games.
- Filling small tables before large tables, which changes who gets the "big table" credit and can unbalance the b_i values.
1620D:
**Key insight.** Any amount X = 3q + r (r ∈ {0,1,2}) can be paid with q value-3 coins plus r small coins, or with (q−1) value-3 coins plus a substitute small-coin combination that also totals 3+r — meaning a small, shared pool of extra 1- and 2-valued coins (at most a couple of each) can flexibly cover whichever residues mod 3 actually occur across all the prices, riding on top of a base supply of value-3 coins sized to the *largest* price.

**Approach.** Fix the value-3 coin count near max(a)//3 (with a possible ±1 adjustment). Case-split on which residues mod 3 actually appear among the prices (plus special handling for any price too small to reach with a value-3 coin at all), and work out the minimal extra 1- and 2-valued coins that simultaneously satisfy every occurring case; take the best resulting configuration.

**Complexity.** O(n) per test case after classifying residues.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Assuming one fixed formula for the extra small coins works regardless of which residue classes appear — different combinations of occurring residues need different small-coin top-ups, and this is a real case-by-case argument, not a single closed form.
- Mishandling very small prices (a_i < 3), which can't always be reached by simply adjusting a value-3 coin.
1555E:
**Key insight.** Point 1 can reach point m through the chosen segments iff *every* unit gap [j, j+1] for j=1..m−1 is covered by at least one selected segment — segments give direct connectivity across their whole span, so end-to-end reachability reduces entirely to "no gap is left completely uncovered." To minimize (max weight − min weight) among chosen segments, sort by weight and slide a two-pointer window.

**Approach.** Sort segments by weight; maintain a range-add/range-minimum structure (segment tree) tracking, per gap, how many currently-included segments cover it. Advance the right pointer, adding each segment's coverage; once every gap has coverage ≥ 1, advance the left pointer as far as possible while the departing segment's own span still keeps coverage ≥ 1 without it (a range-minimum query restricted to just that segment's span); record the weight spread whenever the window fully covers.

**Complexity.** O(n log m), using a segment tree over up to 1e6 points with range-add and range-min.

**Common pitfalls.**
- Re-checking global full coverage on every shrink attempt instead of restricting the check to just the departing segment's own span — the local check is what makes the two-pointer amortized-efficient.
- Off-by-one converting between point coverage and gap coverage (a segment [l, r] covers gaps l..r−1, not l..r).
1567E:
**Key insight.** A segment tree can maintain, per node, everything needed to merge non-decreasing-subarray counts across a boundary: the count fully inside the node, plus the lengths of its longest non-decreasing *prefix* and *suffix*. When merging two children, new cross-boundary non-decreasing subarrays appear exactly when the left child's last element ≤ the right child's first element, contributing (left's suffix length) × (right's prefix length) additional subsegments straddling the join.

**Approach.** Each node stores {count, first value, last value, longest non-decreasing prefix length, longest non-decreasing suffix length}. Merge two children by summing their counts, adding the cross-boundary term when the boundary condition holds, and computing the parent's own prefix/suffix lengths (extended across the boundary when applicable). Point updates touch one leaf and re-merge up to the root; range queries combine the O(log n) covering nodes left-to-right, maintaining a running merged accumulator.

**Complexity.** O((n+q) log n).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Merging query nodes as isolated parent-child pairs instead of accumulating a single running combined state left-to-right — cross-boundary counts between non-adjacent selected nodes get miscounted otherwise.
- Tracking only a suffix length (or only a prefix length) instead of both — both directions are needed since a node may itself be the left or right half of a future merge.
